doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: Jimmy Owens's mentoring after leaving the school principal job
summary: After running a charter school for sixteen years, he returned to music with Jimmy Owens's support and speaks of music's healing power.

venues.name: New York City Department of Education

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Because the technology had changed. Nobody was recording on analog anymore, you know the studios were all set up for digital, all I had were my two boxes with my, you know, and I’m hauling these boxes and stuff, and it was Jon who took me to the studio to take all of that stuff and dump it into digital form. And he oversee’d the process when I would go into the studio, I would come home, I would stay by him and, this is what I got and he would check it out for me. I mean you couldn’t ask for any greater love man. And that’s what I find with these musicians too. You know sometimes you think that you can’t reach them, and these guys are like come, come, come, come learn, come study, come hang out, come, let’s talk. And Jimmy Owens is one of those guys man. I mean Jimmy has mentored me in so many ways. And if it wasn’t for Jimmy, you know I probably would not be out there playing the way I’m playing because when I finished, I was a school principal, I founded a school in Bedford Stuyvesant, the first charter school of the New York City Department of Education which I ran for like about sixteen years. And

when I was finished with that, and it almost took me out, I was really sick and everything, you know I called Jimmy and I said, “Jimmy,” ‘cause I always stayed in touch with Jimmy throughout the years. And I said, “Jimmy, I’m finished man. I’m tired of this thing. I’m not well you know, the school has taken me out, it’s going to take me a while to recover and everything else.” And Jimmy says, “Come in. Come let’s go play music.” And he put me on the bandstand right away. And I think that part of that is that Jimmy also knows how healing that music is. And he told me stories of so many of the guys man, like Lionel, who was so sick, but you put them in front of their instrument and something takes over. And for that moment, that hour, that time, that energy is so healing, it’s so powerful. It keeps them alive. It keeps you young. It helps you to forget the pain. It helps you to forget your suffering. It helps you — you know you communicate with people and people give back you know. Whether it’s in the applause or whether they come up to you and they say hello or they want to touch you or they want — you know they want something. It makes you feel, you know, like life is really worth living in spite of the suffering. And that’s the human condition, right? We’re not, you know, we’re not separate from our suffering. Part of our life is we’re going to go through hardships, whether it’s physical or otherwise. But there’s something that this music brings that helps you to overcome some of your deepest and darkest challenges altogether. And that has to live in the spirit. That has to live in the spirit.
